bib.title: Concentration of Measure (Chapter 5 of Bandit Algorithms)

question: How fast does the sample mean of i.i.d. rewards concentrate around the true mean, in a finite-time form usable to design and analyse bandit algorithms?
contributions: Defines tail probabilities of the sample mean
Defines sigma-subgaussian variables (Def. 5.2) and proves the Cramer-Chernoff tail bound (Thm 5.3), closure properties (Lemma 5.4) and the sample-mean bound (Cor. 5.5)
Notes and exercises give Hoeffding, Bernstein/Bennett, chi-squared, large-deviation and max-of-subgaussians results

results.claim: Theorem 5.3: if X is sigma-subgaussian then for any eps >= 0, P(X >= eps) <= exp(-eps^2/(2 sigma^2)); proof by Markov on exp(lambda X) then lambda = eps/sigma^2. The left tail is symmetric, and the two-sided bound is P(|X|>=eps) <= 2 exp(-eps^2/(2 sigma^2)) by a union bound.
results.quote: Choosing λ = ε/σ2 completes the proof.

Proof left as Exercise 5.7. Exercise 5.8 shows without independence the sum is (sigma1+sigma2)-subgaussian.

results.claim: The CLT rule of thumb that n >= 30 gives a reasonable Gaussian approximation is cautioned against; Bernoulli with p=1/n tends to Poisson(1).
The CLT is asymptotic and so unsuitable for designing bandit algorithms; finite-time bounds need extra assumptions such as subgaussianity.

limits: Proofs of Lemma 5.1, Lemma 5.4, Hoeffding, Bennett and Bernstein are left as exercises; only Theorem 5.3 and Corollary 5.5 are proved in the text.
Subgaussian bound is not tight for Gaussians (misses a 1/sqrt(n eps^2) factor) and a converse constant is admitted loose.
Covers only light-tailed rewards; exponential and chi-squared are not subgaussian (subexponential/subgamma pointed to).
Does not apply a bound to any bandit algorithm: no UCB appears in this chapter.
Textual bounds assume independent samples; adaptively chosen bandit samples need the martingale versions deferred to Ch. 20.
practices: Use the Cramer-Chernoff method (Markov on exp(lambda X), then optimise lambda) to get exponential tails (Thm 5.3).
Prefer finite-time subgaussian bounds over the CLT when designing bandit algorithms (p.76).
State bounds in deviation form (probability 1-delta, radius sqrt(2 sigma^2 log(1/delta)/n)) for convenience (p.78).
Use Hoeffding for bounded rewards and Bernstein/Bennett when variance is small (Notes 4, Ex 5.14).
